effect_estimate.comment: No inferential statistical models, odds ratios, confidence intervals, or p-values are estimated; results consist of descriptive counts/percentages integrated with qualitative key-informant findings.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive mixed-methods findings (no inferential statistical effect estimate reported): across 10 small-town water utilities (piped water coverage ranging from 20% in Awedaya to 85% in Chalanko; n = 630 households), weak institutional oversight and support from higher government offices (irregular Woreda/Zonal meetings, 0/10 utilities with formal risk management programs or operator water-quality records, 0/10 storing emergency spare parts, and delayed emergency support) cascaded into utility staffing, financial, and service weaknesses. Only 4/10 utilities had technicians and financial management personnel, 2/10 monitored water quality, 5/10 chlorinated regularly, and 4/10 had backup generators for grid outages lasting up to 3 months. Although >50% of surveyed households reported paying water bills regularly, un-metered connections, estimated billing due to staff shortages, and meter vandalism undermined cost recovery and system expansion. Service outcomes included seasonal yield shortfalls in 4/10 towns, distribution leaks in 5/10 towns, source microbial contamination up to 26 CFU/100 mL (Bombas) and 168 CFU/100 mL (Fafen), interruptions of 5–15 days/month (Awaday), point-of-use treatment in 9% of households, and household reliance on unimproved sources or private vendors during disruptions.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 3, Study area; PDF pp. 5-8, Results (Sections 1-6); Table 2, PDF p. 6

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by MMAT design ceiling. Assigned 2 because interviews with utility managers, technicians, and Water Board community representatives alongside utility inspections directly document how weak institutional support from service authorities, understaffing, un-metered/estimated tariff billing, delayed emergency procurement, and poor water-energy coordination constrain utility operations, water quality management, cost recovery, and service continuity.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6-8, Results (Sections 3-6); PDF pp. 8-11, Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines utility inability to plan system upgrades, borehole expansion, or climate risk plans (planning), tariff billing via estimates, un-metered connections, and cost-recovery deficits (fees), delayed emergency support/spare-part procurement and untimely utility disruption response (delay), customer mechanisms to report service disruptions (complaint), community representation on town Water Boards (participation), weak oversight/support across regional, Zonal, Woreda, and autonomous utility tiers despite national policy mandates (institutional_fragmentation), and coordination gaps between water utilities, energy departments, and neighbouring towns (political_coordination).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary empirical mixed-methods study combining quantitative data collection (random-sample survey of 630 households, sanitary inspections, microbial and chlorine testing) and qualitative data collection (semi-structured interviews with technicians, utility managers, and board representatives) integrated around the How Tough is WASH framework.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 3-5, Materials and methods (Study approach, Method of data collection, Data analysis)

sample_size.comment: Quantitative survey sampled 630 piped-water households proportionally across 10 purposefully selected towns (Aweday 54, Babile 108, Bombas 60, Chalanko 141, Fafen 12, Haramaya 171, Kersa 34, Kulubi 15, Lange 14, Woter 21). Qualitative interviews included 10 technicians, all town water utility managers, and 10 community board representatives across the 10 utilities.
sample_size.value: 10 town water utilities (10 towns); 630 piped-water households; semi-structured interviews with 10 water supply technicians, all town water utility managers, and 10 community representative Water Board members (1 per town); sanitary inspection and water quality testing of all water sources and reservoirs in the 10 towns

study_design.comment: Applies and adapts the 'How Tough is WASH' climate-resilience framework across 10 small-town water utilities using descriptive quantitative statistics and deductive qualitative coding; no quasi-experimental or randomized intervention comparator.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods cross-sectional study (two rounds in August and December 2022) combining a descriptive random-sample household survey, WHO sanitary risk inspections, microbial and free residual chlorine water quality testing, GIS/DEM flood vulnerability modeling, and deductively coded semi-structured key informant interviews
